Substance
sub'stans
n. (that which stands under; wealth, essence, reality; rendering Hebrew hon, Greek hupostasis)
From the Latin substantia, from sub and sto, to stand under. The Greek hupostasis is built the same way — hupo and histemi — and means that which stands underneath as a foundation, hence both reality and confident assurance.

Biblical Definition

Substance in the Authorized Version carries two senses that the same Latin root holds together. The commoner sense is material wealth: Job's “substance also was seven thousand sheep, and three thousand camels” (Job 1:3), and the prodigal “wasted his substance with riotous living” (Luke 15:13). Proverbs directs this substance godward: “Honour the LORD with thy substance, and with the firstfruits of all thine increase” (Proverbs 3:9) — the firstfruits, not the remainder, which is the whole logic of biblical giving. The second sense is philosophical and far weightier: that which stands under, the underlying reality. Hebrews uses it of faith in one of the most compressed sentences in Scripture: “Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (Hebrews 11:1). Faith is not wishful sentiment about the future; it is the standing-under, the present title-deed, of what God has promised. The same Greek word is used of the Son as the express image of the Father's person, and the Nicene fathers took it up in the term homoousios, of one substance with the Father — the word on which the doctrine of the Trinity turned at Nicaea.

Webster 1828 Definition

That which stands under — hence both a man's material estate and underlying reality itself. Faith is called the substance of things hoped for, and the Son is of one substance with the Father.

expand to see more

SUBSTANCE, n. [L. substantia, of sub and sto, to stand under.] In a general sense, being; something existing by itself; that which underlies accidents.

2. That which constitutes anything what it is; essence; real or essential part.

3. Goods; estate; means; wealth; as, a man of substance.

4. Body; corporeal existence, as distinguished from a shadow.

5. In Scripture, faith is the substance of things hoped for, Heb. 11; honour the Lord with thy substance, Prov. 3.

Key Scripture

Job 1:3 — "His substance also was seven thousand sheep, and three thousand camels, and five hundred yoke of oxen, and five hundred she asses, and a very great household; so that this man was the greatest of all the men of the east."

Proverbs 3:9 — "Honour the LORD with thy substance, and with the firstfruits of all thine increase:"

Hebrews 11:1 — "Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen."

Luke 15:13 — "And not many days after the younger son gathered all together, and took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living."

Modern Corruption

A materialist age keeps the wealth sense and loses the metaphysical one, so that substance means possessions and nothing stands under anything. Scripture uses the word for the unseen reality that upholds the seen.

expand to see more

When only the financial sense survives, Hebrews 11:1 becomes unreadable and gets softened into a statement about optimism — faith as a positive attitude toward an uncertain future. That is precisely what the verse denies. Faith is the hupostasis, the thing standing underneath, of what is hoped for, because the promise of God is more solid than the visible order; the chapter then lists men who staked their lives on it and died without receiving the promises, which no mere optimist does.

The loss also reaches the doctrine of God. Homoousios — of one substance with the Father — was the word Nicaea used to shut out Arianism, and it presupposes that substance means real being rather than stuff. An age that cannot think the category will not defend the creed, and will drift toward a Christ who is functionally divine without being of one substance, which is Arianism with better manners. The principle to recover is that the unseen is not the unreal; the world of goods rests on a reality that goods cannot measure, and the Son upholds all things by the word of his power.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew hon is wealth or sufficiency, and qinyan is acquired property. Greek hupostasis is that which stands under — substance, confidence, title-deed — and ousia is being or essence, the root of homoousios.

expand to see more

Hebrew hon (H1952) — wealth, substance, sufficiency; the word in Proverbs 3:9.

Hebrew qinyan (H7075) — property, acquisition; what a man has got.

Greek hupostasis (G5287) — that which stands under; substance, assurance, confidence.

Greek ousia (G3776) — being, essence, goods; the prodigal wasted his ousia.

Greek homoousios — of one substance; the Nicene term guarding the Son's full deity.

Usage

"Of material estate: his substance also was seven thousand sheep, and three thousand camels (Job 1:3)."

"Of firstfruits giving: honour the LORD with thy substance, and with the firstfruits of all thine increase (Proverbs 3:9)."

"Of faith as underlying reality: faith is the substance of things hoped for (Hebrews 11:1)."
